target_units.text: For the Lord’s eyes are high, but the human being is low; humanity’s height will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.
For the Lord Sabaoth has a day against every insolent and arrogant person, against everyone high and elevated; they will be humbled,
against every cedar of Lebanon among the high and elevated, and against every oak tree of Bashan,
against every mountain and every high hill,
against every high tower and every high wall,
against every ship of the sea and every beautiful display of ships.
Every human being will be humbled, humanity’s height will fall, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.

triples.rationale: Isaiah tells the inhabitants to work their land because ships no longer arrive from Carthage. Ezekiel's maritime lament includes Carthaginian traders before the ship-like city's shattering and the fall of its company. Both describe the collapse of sea commerce; Ezekiel does not give Isaiah's instruction about farming.
triples.source_text: Work your land, for ships no longer come from Carthage.

target_units.text: ships: in them Carthaginians were your traders in abundance among your mixed company. You were filled and became very heavy in the heart of the sea.
Your rowers led you in much water; the south wind shattered you in the heart of the sea.

There were your forces, your payment and that of your mixed companies, your rowers and pilots, your counselors and your mixed companies from your mixed companies, all your warrior men in you, and your whole assembly within you; they will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your fall.

triples.rationale: Isaiah attributes the loss of strength at sea to the Lord's command against Canaan's power. Zechariah names Tyre and Sidon, then announces the Lord's striking Tyre's strength into the sea despite her fortifications and wealth. Both make divine judgment decisive over the coast's maritime strength.
triples.source_text: Your hand no longer has strength at sea, the hand that provoked kings. The Lord Sabaoth commanded concerning Canaan, to destroy her strength.

target_units.text: and Emath within its borders, Tyre and Sidon, because they were exceedingly wise.
Tyre built herself fortifications, stored silver like dust and gathered gold like the mud of the roads.
Therefore the Lord will inherit her and strike her strength into the sea; she will be consumed by fire.

triples.rationale: Isaiah warns that even flight to the Kitians will bring no rest. Deuteronomy likewise describes scattered people finding no rest among foreign nations. The shared condition is refuge failing to provide security; the covenant warning addresses Israel, whereas Isaiah's immediate oracle concerns the coastal population.
triples.source_text: They will say, “You shall no longer continue in insolence and in wronging Sidon’s daughter.” Even if you go to the Kitians, there too you will have no rest,

target_units.text: And the Lord your God shall scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth unto the other; and there you shall serve other gods, wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known.

And among those nations He shall give you no rest, neither shall there be a resting place for the sole of your foot; and the Lord shall give you there a faint heart, and failing eyes, and a wasting soul.

triples.rationale: The warning of no rest in the Chaldeans' devastated land repeats the preceding warning of no rest among the Kitians. Repeating the same outcome for two possible destinations closes off the expectation that another foreign refuge will escape the announced calamity.
triples.source_text: and into the Chaldeans’ land: this too has been devastated by the Assyrians. There too you will have no rest, because her wall has fallen.

target_units.text: They will say, “You shall no longer continue in insolence and in wronging Sidon’s daughter.” Even if you go to the Kitians, there too you will have no rest,

triples.rationale: Isaiah commands Carthage's ships to wail because their fortress has perished. Ezekiel portrays rowers leaving their ships, maritime people standing ashore and raising a bitter cry, followed by a lament over Tyre. Both turn the trading fleet into mourners for the fallen city.
triples.source_text: Wail, ships of Carthage, because your fortress has perished!

target_units.text: and all your rowers will come down from the ships; the passengers and the lookouts of the sea will stand on the land.
They will raise a cry over you with their voice and cry bitterly; they will put earth on their head and spread ashes beneath them.
Their sons will take up a lament over you and a lamentation for you:

triples.rationale: Isaiah assigns Tyre seventy years of being left before her condition changes. Jeremiah also marks a period of national humiliation and service by seventy years, followed by divine action. The shared bounded duration is explicit, but the two passages concern different subjects and do not establish an identical chronology.
triples.source_text: On that day Tyre will be left for seventy years, like a king’s time, like a person’s time. After seventy years, Tyre will be like a prostitute’s song:

target_units.text: And all the land will become a ruin, and they will serve among the nations for seventy years.
And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will exact justice from that nation, says the Lord, and make them an everlasting ruin.

triples.rationale: Isaiah promises that Tyre will return to her former state as a trading center for the world's kingdoms. Ezekiel identifies Tyre as the sea's entrance and trading place for peoples from many islands. That portrait makes concrete the international commercial role Isaiah says will be restored.
triples.source_text: After seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she will again be restored to her former state and become a trading center for all the inhabited world’s kingdoms.

target_units.text: and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrance of the sea, the trading place of the peoples from many islands: Thus says the Lord to Tyre: You said, ‘I have clothed myself with my beauty.’

triples.relationship: foreign wealth consecrated to the Lord
triples.rationale: Isaiah dedicates Tyre's trade and wages to the Lord and to the support of those dwelling before Him. Isaiah 60 likewise brings sea and national wealth toward Zion, culminating in acceptable offerings and the glorification of God's house. Both redirect international prosperity toward the Lord's service.
triples.source_text: Her trade and her wage will be holy to the Lord. It will not be collected for them; instead, all her trade will be for those dwelling before the Lord, to eat and drink and be filled, as a contribution, a memorial before the Lord.

target_units.text: Then you will see and fear and be astonished in heart, for the wealth of sea, nations, and peoples will turn toward you. There will come to you
herds of camels, and camels from Madiam and Gaipha will cover you. They will all come from Saba, bringing gold and carrying frankincense, and they will proclaim the Lord’s salvation as good news.
All Kedar’s sheep will gather to you, and Nabaioth’s rams will come to you. They will be offered acceptably upon My altar, and My house of prayer will be glorified.

triples.rationale: Isaiah announces the Lord's devastation of the inhabited world and scattering of its residents. Zephaniah similarly announces the removal of humanity and other creatures from the earth's face. Both use comprehensive earthly destruction to introduce divine judgment, without restricting Isaiah's statement to one named city.
triples.source_text: Behold, the Lord is destroying the inhabited world; He will make it desolate, uncover its face and scatter those dwelling in it.

target_units.text: Let everything utterly disappear from the face of the earth, says the Lord,
let humanity and livestock disappear, let birds of the sky and fish of the sea disappear, and I will remove people from the face of the earth, says the Lord.

triples.rationale: Isaiah places people and priest under the same impending condition before listing other social pairs. Hosea likewise says the people will be like the priest in a sentence of recompense. Both remove the expectation that priestly position exempts someone from the people's judgment.
triples.source_text: The people will be like the priest, the slave like the master, the maidservant like the mistress; the buyer will be like the seller, the lender like the borrower, and the debtor like the one to whom he owes a debt.

target_units.text: It will be as with the people, so with the priest; I will exact punishment upon him for his ways and repay him for his schemes.

triples.rationale: Isaiah says buyer and seller will share the same condition when judgment comes. Ezekiel warns the buyer not to rejoice and the seller not to lament when the appointed day arrives, because ordinary exchange no longer offers security. Both suspend the usual contrast between commercial gain and loss.
triples.source_text: The people will be like the priest, the slave like the master, the maidservant like the mistress; the buyer will be like the seller, the lender like the borrower, and the debtor like the one to whom he owes a debt.

target_units.text: The time has come; behold, the day! Let the buyer not rejoice, nor the seller lament;
for the buyer certainly will no longer return to the seller, and a person will not prevail in the eye of his life.

triples.rationale: Isaiah grounds the earth's destruction in what the Lord's mouth has spoken. Peter similarly places the present world under a judgment reserved by God's word, recalling the earlier world's destruction by water. The connection is divine speech and world judgment; Peter specifies water and fire, which this Isaiah unit does not.
triples.source_text: The earth will be utterly destroyed, and the earth utterly plundered, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken these things.

target_units.text: through which the world that then existed was flooded with water and perished.
But the present heavens and earth have been stored up by the same word for fire, kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly people.

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes the earth and its high inhabitants mourning under devastation. Hosea likewise makes the land mourn and diminish together with its inhabitants because of their offenses. Both present the land as participating in the consequences of human wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: The earth mourned, the inhabited world was destroyed, and the earth’s high ones mourned.

target_units.text: Therefore the land will mourn and diminish with all who inhabit it, with the field’s beasts, the earth’s creeping things and heaven’s birds; the sea’s fish will disappear,

triples.rationale: Isaiah explains the earth's lawlessness through transgressed law and changed ordinances and covenant. Leviticus connects refusal of God's judgments and commandments, dissolving His covenant, with ensuing distress. The shared covenantal pattern is explicit, while Isaiah's wider earthly scope is not reduced to every detail of Leviticus's penalties.
triples.source_text: The earth acted lawlessly because of those dwelling in it, because they transgressed the law and changed the ordinances, an everlasting covenant.

target_units.text: but disobey them, and your soul is indignant at My judgments, so that you do not do all My commandments, so as to dissolve My covenant,
then I will do this to you: I will bring distress upon you, scab and jaundice that waste your eyes and melt away your life. You shall sow your seeds in vain, and your adversaries shall eat them.

triples.rationale: Isaiah says a curse follows the inhabitants' sin and leaves few people. Deuteronomy likewise warns that disobedience will leave the formerly numerous people few in number. Both connect culpable refusal of God with the drastic reduction of a population.
triples.source_text: Therefore a curse will consume the earth, because those dwelling in it sinned. Therefore those dwelling on the earth will be poor, and few people will be left.

target_units.text: And you shall be left few in number, whereas you were as the stars of heaven in multitude, because you did not hearken unto the voice of the Lord your God.

triples.rationale: Isaiah makes wine and vine mourn while those who bring gladness groan. Joel likewise describes ruined agricultural produce and a dried vine, saying human beings have put joy to shame. Both join vine and wine imagery with troubled human gladness, while Joel's stated causal wording is preserved.
triples.source_text: Wine will mourn, the vine will mourn, and all who gladden the soul will groan.

target_units.text: because the plains have suffered. Let the earth mourn, because grain has suffered, wine has dried up, and oil has diminished.
The farmers have dried up. Lament, estates, over wheat and barley, because the harvest from the field has perished.
The vine has dried up and the fig trees have diminished; pomegranate, palm, apple tree and all the field’s trees have dried up, because human beings have put joy to shame.

triples.rationale: Isaiah lists the end of tambourine joy and the lyre's sound among judgment's effects. Ezekiel's sentence upon Tyre likewise ends its musicians and the audible sound of psalteries. The shared image is a formerly festive community made musically silent by destruction.
triples.source_text: The joy of tambourines has ceased; the impudence and wealth of the ungodly have ceased; the lyre’s sound has ceased.

target_units.text: He will put an end to the multitude of your musicians, and the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard.

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes every city deserted and a house shut against entry. Jeremiah similarly depicts inhabitants fleeing at the sound of horseman and bow until every city is abandoned and no one dwells in them. Both portray judgment through empty urban habitation, though Jeremiah names the immediate military cause.
triples.source_text: Every city was deserted; he will shut a house so that none may enter.

target_units.text: At the sound of a horseman and a drawn bow the whole countryside withdrew; they entered caves and hid in groves and climbed onto the rocks. Every city was abandoned; no human dwells in them.

triples.rationale: Isaiah commands lament over wine because the earth's gladness has ceased. Joel calls wine drinkers to weep and lament because gladness and joy have been removed from their mouths. The combination of wine, commanded mourning and lost joy makes the correspondence specific.
triples.source_text: Wail over wine everywhere! All the earth’s gladness has ceased.

target_units.text: Sober up, you drunkards, from their wine, and weep! Lament, all who drink wine to intoxication, because gladness and joy have been removed from your mouths.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 24 leaves cities deserted and abandoned houses perishing. The answer to Isaiah's earlier question about duration likewise describes cities without inhabitants, houses without people and a desolate land. Both define the severity of judgment through the disappearance of settled human life.
triples.source_text: Cities will be left deserted, and abandoned houses will perish.

target_units.text: And I said, How long, O Lord? And He said: Until cities lie waste, without inhabitants, and houses, without people, and the land is left desolate.
And after these things God will remove people far away; and those who remain will multiply upon the land.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 24 compares the nations under judgment to an olive tree gleaned after harvest. Isaiah 17 spells out the same image as a few berries remaining on high branches. The earlier description clarifies how a gleaned tree can portray the small remainder after devastation.
triples.source_text: All these things will happen on the earth, among the nations: as when someone gleans an olive tree, so they will glean them, even when the grape harvest has ceased.

target_units.text: and a stalk is left in it, or like olive berries, two or three on a lofty top, or four or five left on their branches. Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God.

triples.rationale: Those left on the earth rejoice with the Lord's glory in Isaiah 24. Isaiah 12 calls Zion's inhabitants to sing, announce His glorious deeds and rejoice because Israel's Holy One is exalted among them. Both place communal praise of the Lord's glory within a setting of salvation after distress.
triples.source_text: These will cry aloud, and those left upon the earth will rejoice together with the Lord’s glory. The sea’s water will be troubled;

target_units.text: On that day you will say, “Sing hymns to the Lord, cry out His name, announce His glorious deeds among the nations, remember that His name was exalted.
Sing the Lord’s name, because He has done exalted things; announce these throughout the earth.
Exult and be glad, you who dwell in Zion, because Israel’s Holy One has been exalted in her midst.”

triples.rationale: Isaiah 24 places the Lord's glory and glorious name in the sea's islands. Isaiah 42 explicitly summons islands, sea travelers and distant inhabitants to glorify His name and announce His deeds. Both extend the Lord's praise beyond the land to maritime peoples.
triples.source_text: therefore the Lord’s glory will be in the sea’s islands; the Lord’s name will be glorious—O Lord, Israel’s God!

target_units.text: Sing a new hymn to the Lord—its beginning: “Glorify His name from the earth’s extremity, you who go down to the sea and sail it, islands and their inhabitants.”
Rejoice, wilderness and its villages, settlements and those inhabiting Kedar. Those inhabiting Petra will rejoice and cry out from the mountain tops.
They will give God glory and announce His praiseworthy deeds in the islands.

triples.relationship: contrasting destinies of the devout and impious
triples.rationale: Isaiah's report couples hope for the devout with woe for rejecters of the law. Proverbs likewise preserves hope for the righteous while the impious person's boast perishes. Both contrast hope for the righteous with calamity for the ungodly; Proverbs specifically frames its contrast at death.
triples.source_text: From the earth’s wings we heard wonders: “Hope for the devout!” And they will say, “Woe to those who reject, those who reject the law!”

target_units.text: When a righteous man dies, hope does not perish, but the boast of the impious perishes.

triples.rationale: Isaiah announces fear, pit and trap upon the earth's inhabitant. Jeremiah uses the same three dangers, in a different order, against resident Moab. The tightly shared formulation depicts inescapable danger, while the addressed population differs.
triples.source_text: Fear, pit and trap are upon you who dwell on the earth!

target_units.text: Trap, fear, and pit are upon you, resident Moab.

triples.rationale: Both passages say that fleeing fear leads into a pit and climbing from the pit leads into a trap. Jeremiah directs the sequence against Moab in her visitation year, whereas Isaiah places it within upheaval of earth and heaven. The successive failed escapes are a close verbal and structural parallel.
triples.source_text: Whoever flees the fear will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught by the trap, because windows from heaven have opened and the earth’s foundations will be shaken.

target_units.text: One who flees from fear will fall into the pit, and one who climbs from the pit will be caught in the trap, for I will bring these things upon Moab in the year of her visitation.

triples.rationale: Isaiah connects the failed escapes with heaven's opened windows and shaken earthly foundations. Genesis describes the opening of heaven's floodgates when the flood begins. Both use openings above as a sign of catastrophic judgment; Isaiah's unit is not thereby identified as a second narration of Noah's flood.
triples.source_text: Whoever flees the fear will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught by the trap, because windows from heaven have opened and the earth’s foundations will be shaken.

target_units.text: In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the deep burst open, and the floodgates of heaven were opened.

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes the earth utterly agitated and at a loss. Hebrews discusses God's shaking of earth and heaven and the removal of created things that can be shaken. Both make shaking an image of the created order's inability to remain secure before divine action; no direct quotation of this Isaiah verse is claimed.
triples.source_text: The earth will be utterly agitated, and the earth will be utterly at a loss;

target_units.text: His voice shook the earth then, but now He has promised, saying, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven.”
Now “yet once more” indicates the removal of the things shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things not shaken may remain.

triples.rationale: Isaiah pictures the earth tilting and shaking before an irreversible fall under lawlessness. The psalm also speaks of God shaking and fracturing the earth, but pleads for its healing. The shared physical image supports the comparison while the plea for repair and announced final collapse remain distinct.
triples.source_text: The earth has tilted and will be shaken like a fruit-watcher’s shelter, like someone drunk and hungover. It will fall and will never be able to rise, for lawlessness has prevailed upon it.

target_units.text: Thou didst shake the earth and trouble it; heal its fractures, for it was shaken.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 24 directs God's hand against heaven's array as well as earthly kings. Isaiah 34 depicts heaven rolling up and its stars falling. Both extend the imagery of divine judgment to the heavenly order, without requiring a particular identification of the array with named spiritual beings.
triples.source_text: God will bring His hand against heaven’s array and against the earth’s kings.

target_units.text: Heaven will roll up like a scroll, and all the stars will fall like leaves from a vine, like leaves falling from a fig tree.

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes confinement in a fortress and prison followed much later by visitation. Peter describes sinful angels confined in gloom and kept for judgment. Both present restraint before subsequent divine reckoning; Isaiah's visitation is not called release, and its prisoners are not equated with Peter's angels.
triples.source_text: They will gather and shut them into a fortress and a prison; after many generations there will be a visitation of them.

target_units.text: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into Tartarus and handed them over to chains of gloom, kept for judgment,

triples.rationale: Isaiah says the Lord will reign in Zion and Jerusalem and be glorified before the elders. Micah likewise promises that the Lord will reign over the gathered remnant on Mount Zion. Both place the Lord's rule on Zion beyond the surrounding scenes of affliction and judgment.
triples.source_text: The brick will melt and the wall will fall, because the Lord will reign in Zion and in Jerusalem and will be glorified before the elders.

target_units.text: I will make the crushed one a remnant and the rejected one a strong nation. The Lord will reign over them on Mount Zion from now and forever.

triples.rationale: Isaiah promises to glorify God and sing His name because He has done wondrous things. The psalm likewise calls for a new song because the Lord has done wonders and worked salvation. In both, accomplished divine wonders are the stated reason for singing praise.
triples.source_text: Lord my God, I will glorify Thee and sing Thy name, because Thou hast done wondrous things, an ancient, true plan. May it be so, Lord!

target_units.text: A psalm of David. Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done wonders. His right hand and His holy arm won salvation for Him.

triples.rationale: Isaiah's praise names God's wondrous action as an ancient, true plan. Isaiah 46 declares that God's counsel will stand and that He will do all He has planned, announcing outcomes before they happen. Both connect trustworthy divine planning with events brought to completion.
triples.source_text: Lord my God, I will glorify Thee and sing Thy name, because Thou hast done wondrous things, an ancient, true plan. May it be so, Lord!

target_units.text: announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’

triples.rationale: Isaiah celebrates the reduction of fortified cities and says the ungodly city will never be rebuilt. Ezekiel similarly pronounces that Tyre will become bare rock and will not be rebuilt. The shared feature is irreversible urban ruin; Isaiah's unnamed city is not identified as Tyre solely from that resemblance.
triples.source_text: For Thou hast made cities a mound, fortified cities so that their foundations fall. The city of the ungodly will certainly never be rebuilt.

target_units.text: I will make you a smooth rock, a drying place for nets. You will certainly not be rebuilt, for I have spoken, says the Lord.

triples.rationale: Isaiah says poor people and wronged communities will bless God. The psalm calls the poor to rejoice because the Lord hears the needy and does not despise His bound ones. Both make the response of the disadvantaged central to praise for divine help.
triples.source_text: Therefore the poor people will bless Thee, and cities of wronged people will bless Thee.

target_units.text: Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul will live,
for the Lord heard the needy and did not despise His bound ones.

triples.rationale: Isaiah calls God a helper and shelter for lowly, needy and wronged people. The psalm likewise names the Lord a refuge for the needy and helper in distress. The correspondence concerns God's particular protection of the vulnerable rather than an unspecified claim of help.
triples.source_text: For Thou didst become a helper to every lowly city and a shelter to those discouraged by need. Thou wilt rescue them from evil people, a shelter for the thirsty and a breath for wronged people.

target_units.text: And the Lord became a refuge for the needy, a helper at fitting times in distress.

triples.rationale: Isaiah portrays fainthearted, thirsty people blessing God amid oppression, following the promise of His shelter. The psalm recounts hungry, thirsty people whose strength fails, their cry and rescue, and a call to acknowledge God's mercies. Both bring thanksgiving out of the distress pictured through thirst and weakness.
triples.source_text: They will bless Thee like fainthearted people thirsting in Zion because of ungodly people, to whom Thou didst hand us over.

target_units.text: hungry and thirsty; their soul failed within them.
They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He rescued them from their distresses,
and guided them into a straight way to travel to a city of habitation.
Let them acknowledge to the Lord His mercies and His wonders to the sons of men,

triples.rationale: Isaiah promises gladness and wine for all nations on the Lord's mountain. Jesus speaks of many arriving from east and west to recline with the patriarchs in the kingdom. Both envision people beyond a single local community sharing a celebratory divine welcome; Isaiah's native wording about wine and perfume is preserved.
triples.source_text: The Lord Sabaoth will act for all the nations upon this mountain. They will drink gladness, drink wine and anoint themselves with perfume.

target_units.text: I tell you that many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of the heavens,

triples.rationale: Isaiah says the plan on this mountain concerns all nations. Isaiah 2 likewise gathers nations to the Lord's mountain for His instruction and judgment. The connection is the mountain as the setting of God's purpose for the nations; this source unit is not described as mentioning a veil or shroud.
triples.source_text: On this mountain, hand all these things over to the nations, for this plan concerns all the nations.

target_units.text: In the last days the Lord’s mountain and God’s house will be clearly visible on the summits of the mountains and be raised above the hills; all the nations will come to it,

and many nations will go and say, “Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain and to the house of Jacob’s God. He will announce His way to us, and we will walk in it.” For law will go out from Zion, and the Lord’s word from Jerusalem.

He will judge between the nations and reprove a numerous people. They will beat their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will no longer take sword against nation, and they will certainly no longer learn to wage war.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 25 says God removes every tear from every face and takes away His people's reproach. Isaiah 65 likewise promises that weeping and crying will no longer be heard in the restored Jerusalem. Both describe the removal of communal sorrow by God, without altering Isaiah 25's distinctive preceding statement about death.
triples.source_text: Death swallowed, having prevailed; and again God removed every tear from every face. He removed the people’s reproach from all the earth, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken.

target_units.text: I will exult over Jerusalem and rejoice over My people, and no sound of weeping or crying will ever again be heard in her.

triples.rationale: Isaiah's people recognize their God and rejoice in the salvation for which they hoped. The psalm calls for rejoicing in the Lord's day, cries for salvation and acknowledges that the Lord God has shone upon His people. Both join communal joy, divine recognition and salvation in worship.
triples.source_text: On that day they will say, “Behold, our God, in whom we hoped and exulted; and we will rejoice in our salvation.”

target_units.text: This is the day the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it.
O Lord, save now! O Lord, prosper us now!
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord. We have blessed you from the house of the Lord.
The Lord is God, and He has shone upon us. Arrange a festival among the thickly covering boughs, up to the horns of the altar.

triples.rationale: Isaiah compares Moab's trampling to the treading of a threshing floor. Micah gathers hostile nations like sheaves and commands Zion to thresh them. Both employ the crushing action of threshing to picture defeat of hostile peoples, while their named agents and immediate targets differ.
triples.source_text: For God will give rest upon this mountain, and Moab’s land will be trampled as people tread a threshing floor with wagons,

target_units.text: But they did not know the Lord’s thought or understand His counsel, for He gathered them like sheaves of a threshing floor.

Rise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze. With them you will melt down nations and grind many peoples fine; you will dedicate their multitude to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.

triples.rationale: Within the oracle against Moab, Isaiah 25 announces the bringing down of insolence. Isaiah 16 likewise names Moab's excessive insolence and arrogance before its country-wide lament. Both connect Moab's humiliation with the pride that preceded it.
triples.source_text: and he will release his hands, just as he himself brought low for destruction; he will bring low his insolence over what he laid his hands on,

target_units.text: We heard Moab’s insolence—exceedingly insolent. You raised up your arrogance. Your divination is not so,
not so. Moab will wail, for all in Moab’s country will wail. You will ponder for Deseth’s residents and not be ashamed.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 25 brings the height of the wall's refuge down to the ground. The following song likewise says God brings down those dwelling high and casts fortified cities to the ground. The repeated movement from elevated defenses to ground level links the adjoining judgment descriptions.
triples.source_text: and he will bring low the height of your wall’s refuge, and it will descend to the ground.

target_units.text: Thou who didst humble and bring down those dwelling on high. Thou wilt cast down fortified cities and bring them to the ground,

triples.rationale: Isaiah 26 makes salvation a wall and encircling wall for the fortified city. Isaiah 60 similarly names the restored city's walls Salvation. Both portray the community's saving security through city defenses, rather than treating physical fortification alone as the source of safety.
triples.source_text: On that day they will sing this song in Judah’s land, saying, “Behold, a fortified city! He will make our salvation a wall and an encircling wall.

target_units.text: Injustice will no longer be heard in your land, nor destruction and misery within your borders. Your walls will be called Salvation, and your gates Engraving.

triples.rationale: Isaiah commands the gates to open for a people keeping righteousness and truth. The psalm asks for the gates of righteousness to open and declares that the righteous enter the Lord's gate. Both connect admission through the gates with the character of the entering worshipers.
triples.source_text: Open the gates; let a people enter, keeping righteousness and keeping truth,

target_units.text: Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will give thanks to the Lord.
This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous will enter through it.

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes people holding truth and keeping peace, with their hope in God expressed across this verse and the next.
